tips.title: Four stages, transport in all of them
tips.body: An LCA covers **extracting and processing raw materials**, **manufacturing and packaging**, **use and operation during its lifetime**, **disposal at the end of its useful life** — and **transport and distribution at each stage**. Transport is not a fifth box; it is counted inside every one of the four.

tips.title: LCA is not purely objective
tips.body: Water, resources, energy and some wastes can be **quantified** fairly easily. Putting a **number on a pollutant effect** requires **value judgements**, so an LCA is **not a purely objective process**. That sentence is worth learning — it is the point examiners most want.

tips.title: Selective LCAs can be misused
tips.body: An **abbreviated** or **selective** LCA leaves stages out. That can be legitimate shorthand, but it can also be **misused to reach a pre-determined conclusion** — for instance to support an **advertising** claim. Ask which stages were left out and who benefits.

tips.title: Reduce, reuse, recycle — in that order
tips.body: **Reducing** use saves the most, because nothing is made at all. **Reuse** keeps the object as it is — a glass bottle refilled. **Recycling** breaks it down and remakes it, which still costs energy. All three cut the use of limited resources, energy, waste and environmental impact.

tips.title: Recycling skips the extraction stage
tips.body: Recycling a metal means melting and recasting it, which avoids **mining the ore, transporting it and extracting the metal** — by far the most energy-hungry stage. Scrap steel added to blast furnace iron reduces the amount that has to come from ore at all.

why.matters:
Which is better for the environment, a plastic bag or a cotton one? Intuition answers immediately and is often wrong, because it counts only the part of the story you can see — the bag in your hand, not the field, the factory or the lorry.

A **life cycle assessment** is the attempt to count all of it: raw materials, manufacture, use, disposal. It is the most useful thing in this unit and the least certain, because some of what it counts has to be **judged** rather than measured.

examples.title: Which bag is actually better?
examples.body:
A plastic carrier is cheap to make and lasts for ever in a hedge. A cotton tote is grown, irrigated, dyed and shipped, and then rots away in a year.

The two answers point in opposite directions, which is exactly why the assessment has to cover the **whole life**. The cotton bag costs far more to make and far less to throw away, so it only comes out ahead once it has been used enough times — and how many times that is depends on what you count. A bag used once is the worst of both.

visual.alt: A table comparing a plastic bag and a cotton bag at each stage of their lives: crude oil against a crop and water, little energy to make against a great deal, one or two uses against hundreds, and lasting for ever against rotting

examples.title: Why aluminium is the one everybody recycles
examples.body:
Making aluminium from its ore means electrolysis: a cell at 950 °C with a current running through it, and the electricity is the reducing agent rather than an overhead.

Recycling it means **melting** it, at 660 °C, and casting it again. The chemistry is skipped entirely, because the metal is already metal — and unlike paper, which loses fibre length every time, aluminium is not degraded by the trip. A can can become a can indefinitely, which is not true of most materials.

boxes.title: From ore
boxes.body: Electrolysis, and the electricity is the reagent.

boxes.title: From cans
boxes.body: Melt at 660 °C and cast it again.

boxes.title: No decline
boxes.body: Unlike paper, it is not degraded by reuse.

visual.alt: Four boxes round a centre reading the same metal twice: getting aluminium from ore needs electrolysis with the electricity as the reagent, while recycling it only needs melting at six hundred and sixty degrees, with no chemistry and no loss of quality

examples.title: Why two honest assessments disagree
examples.body:
Some of an assessment is measurement: how much energy a furnace used, how much water a field needed, how far the lorry drove. Those numbers can be checked.

The rest is **judgement**. How do you weigh a tonne of carbon dioxide against a hectare of habitat, or damage now against damage in fifty years? Where do you stop counting? Two careful people can answer those differently and reach opposite conclusions from the same data.

Which is also how the other kind happens: an assessment that counts only the stages that suit the seller is not an assessment, and the specification calls it advertising.

visual.alt: A table separating what a life cycle assessment can measure, such as the energy used and the tonnes of waste produced, from what has to be judged, such as how much each of those matters and where to stop counting

steps.title: Finite resources and sustainable development
steps.body:
Humans use the Earth's resources for **warmth, shelter, food and transport**. Natural resources, supplemented by **agriculture**, provide food, timber, clothing and fuels, while **finite resources** from the Earth, the oceans and the atmosphere are processed into energy and materials.

**Finite or renewable?**

- A **finite** resource is one that is **not being replaced**, or is replaced far more slowly than it is used — crude oil, metal ores, natural gas.
- A **renewable** resource is replaced at the rate it is used, or faster — timber from replanted forests, cotton, wool.

Some natural products are **supplemented or replaced by agricultural and synthetic products**: rubber can come from a tree or from crude oil; cotton is agricultural, polyester synthetic.

**Sustainable development** is **development that meets the needs of current generations without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.**

Chemistry contributes by improving agricultural and industrial processes, and by finding ways to use **less** of a finite resource for the same result — which is what the rest of this topic is about.

steps.title: Life cycle assessment
steps.body:
A **life cycle assessment** (LCA) works out the **environmental impact of a product** across its whole life, not just while it is being used.

**The four stages:**

1. **Extracting and processing raw materials**
2. **Manufacturing and packaging**
3. **Use and operation during its lifetime**
4. **Disposal at the end of its useful life**

and **transport and distribution at each stage** — counted within all four, not added as a fifth.

**What can be measured, and what cannot.** Use of **water**, **use of resources**, **use of energy sources**, **production of some wastes** can be **fairly easily quantified**. But **allocating numerical values to pollutant effects** is **less straightforward and requires value judgements** — how do you score a unit of smog against a unit of habitat loss?

So an **LCA is not a purely objective process**. Two honest assessors can reach different conclusions from the same data because they weight the pollutants differently.

**Selective and abbreviated LCAs.** A shortened LCA can be devised to evaluate a product, but these **can be misused to reach pre-determined conclusions** — for example **in support of claims for advertising purposes**. A company can choose the stages that flatter its product and omit the rest.

steps.title: Comparing plastic and paper shopping bags
steps.body: AQA asks for **simple comparative LCAs for shopping bags made from plastic and paper**. Work stage by stage, and notice that the answer depends on how often each bag is used.

visuals.problem: Compare a plastic bag and a paper bag across the four LCA stages.

steps.text: **Raw materials.** Plastic comes from **crude oil**, a finite resource. Paper comes from **timber**, which is renewable if forests are replanted.
steps.note: renewable does not automatically mean better

steps.text: **Manufacturing.** Making paper uses **more energy and much more water** than making a plastic bag, and the plastic bag is lighter.
steps.note: this is where paper does badly

steps.text: **Use.** A plastic bag is **stronger and waterproof**, so it can be **reused many times**; a paper bag tears and is often used once.
**Disposal.** Paper is **biodegradable and easily recycled**; plastic **does not biodegrade** and may persist in the environment for a very long time.
steps.note: this is where plastic does badly

steps.text: **Conclusion.** On energy the plastic bag starts ahead: the paper bag would have to be used **4 times** to bring its energy per use down to one plastic bag's, and paper bags tear. So the verdict depends on how each bag is used, not only on the material.
steps.note: a comparative LCA must state its assumption

props.title: Each material wins two stages, so the conclusion depends on reuse

check.prompt: A paper bag takes 2.0 units of energy to make and a plastic bag 0.5 units. How many times must the paper bag be used for its energy per use to match a plastic bag used once?
check.solution: $\dfrac{2.0}{0.5} = $ **4 times**. Used fewer times than that, the paper bag costs more energy per use than a single plastic bag. The plastic bag never needs a second use to be ahead on energy: $0.5 < 2.0$ already.

steps.title: Reducing, reusing and recycling
steps.body:
**Reduction in use, reuse and recycling** of materials by end users **reduces the use of limited resources, the use of energy sources, waste and environmental impacts.**

**Why it matters.** **Metals, glass, building materials, clay ceramics and most plastics** are produced from **limited raw materials**. Much of the **energy** for those processes also comes from limited resources, and obtaining raw materials by **quarrying and mining causes environmental impacts**.

**Reuse.** Some products, such as **glass bottles**, can be **reused** — washed and refilled, with no chemical change at all. That is the cheapest option in energy terms.

**Recycling glass.** Where a bottle cannot be reused, it can be **crushed and melted to make different glass products**.

**Recycling metals.** Metals are recycled by **melting and recasting or reforming into different products**. This skips the extraction stage entirely — no ore mined, no ore transported, no reduction of the ore. For a metal like aluminium the saving is large: if extracting from ore costs 100 units and recycling 5, recycling saves **95%** of the energy.

**How much separation is needed** depends on **the material and the properties required of the final product**. Some uses need a pure metal; others do not. For example, **some scrap steel can be added to iron from a blast furnace**, reducing the amount of iron that has to be extracted from **iron ore**.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Name all four stages, and put transport inside them.** An answer that lists three, or that treats transport as a separate stage, loses marks. The phrase is *transport and distribution **at each stage***.

**Explain the objectivity point precisely.** Not "LCAs can be biased" but *allocating numerical values to **pollutant effects** requires **value judgements**, so the process is not purely objective*. The measurable things — water, resources, energy, some wastes — should be named alongside.

**Say who benefits from a selective LCA.** A shortened assessment that omits the stages where a product does badly can support an **advertising** claim. Identifying the missing stage is the analytical move.

**Keep reuse and recycling apart.** Reusing a bottle involves **no chemical change** and no remaking; recycling it means **crushing and melting**. Reuse saves more energy, and questions test the distinction directly.

**Quantify where you can.** If a question gives energy figures, calculate the break-even number of uses rather than describing the trade-off in words. $2 \div 0.5 = 4$ is a stronger answer than "it depends".

**Do not assume renewable means better.** Paper comes from a renewable resource yet uses **more energy and water** to make. The LCA is the whole picture, not the first stage.

**Link recycling to the extraction stage.** The saving comes from **not mining, transporting or reducing the ore** — that is the specific reason, and it also explains why the saving is largest for metals that are expensive to extract.

**Mention that separation depends on the end use.** Scrap steel can go straight into a blast furnace charge because the product tolerates it; a use needing pure metal would require more sorting.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Finite** resources are not replaced as fast as they are used; **renewable** ones are.
- **Sustainable development** meets **present needs without compromising future generations**.
- **LCA stages**: **extracting and processing raw materials**; **manufacturing and packaging**; **use and operation during its lifetime**; **disposal at the end of its useful life** — plus **transport and distribution at each stage**.
- Easily quantified: **use of water**, **use of resources**, **use of energy sources**, **production of some wastes**.
- **Allocating numerical values to pollutant effects** requires **value judgements**, so an LCA is **not purely objective**.
- **Selective or abbreviated LCAs** can be **misused to reach pre-determined conclusions**, for example for **advertising**.
- **Reduce, reuse, recycle** all cut the use of limited resources, energy, waste and environmental impact.
- **Glass bottles** can be **reused**, or **crushed and melted** into different glass products.
- **Metals** are recycled by **melting and recasting or reforming**.
- Recycling avoids **mining, transporting and extracting from ore**, the most energy-hungry stage.
- The **separation** needed depends on the **material and the properties required**.
- **Scrap steel** added to blast furnace iron reduces the iron extracted from ore.
- A comparative LCA of bags depends on **how often each is reused**.

questions.prompt:
A supermarket claims its new paper bags are "better for the environment" than the plastic bags they replace.

Describe how a life cycle assessment would test this claim, and explain why two assessors might reach different conclusions from the same data. (6 marks)
questions.solution:
A life cycle assessment would examine four stages: **extracting and processing the raw materials**, **manufacturing and packaging**, **use and operation during the bag's lifetime**, and **disposal at the end of its useful life** — with **transport and distribution counted at each stage**.

Applied to the bags: the plastic comes from **crude oil**, a **finite** resource, while paper comes from **timber**, which is renewable if forests are replanted — so paper wins the first stage. But **manufacturing** paper uses **more energy and much more water**, so plastic wins the second. In **use**, a plastic bag is stronger and waterproof and can be **reused many times**, while a paper bag often tears after one trip. On **disposal**, paper is **biodegradable and easily recycled**, whereas plastic **does not biodegrade** and may persist for a very long time.

Much of this can be **quantified fairly easily** — the **water, resources and energy** used, and the **wastes produced**. That part of the assessment is objective.

Two assessors can still disagree, because **allocating numerical values to pollutant effects requires value judgements**. How many litres of water saved is worth one plastic bag persisting in the sea? There is no measurement that settles it, so an assessor who weights water use heavily will favour plastic, and one who weights persistent waste heavily will favour paper. This is why an LCA is **not a purely objective process**.

The supermarket's claim should therefore be checked for which stages its assessment covered. A **selective or abbreviated LCA** omitting the manufacturing stage would flatter paper, and such assessments **can be misused to reach pre-determined conclusions in support of advertising claims**.

examTechnique.body:
An LCA covers **four stages** — raw materials, manufacture and packaging, use, disposal — with **transport and distribution at each**. Water, resources, energy and some wastes can be **quantified**; **pollutant effects require value judgements**, so an LCA is **not purely objective**.

examinerErrors: Treating transport as a fifth stage.
Saying LCAs are "biased" without naming value judgements.
Assuming a renewable raw material makes the whole product better.
Saying recycling "saves energy" without saying which stage is avoided.
Describing a trade-off in words when figures are given.
Not identifying which stages a selective LCA has omitted.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer names all four stages with transport inside each, separates what can be measured from what needs a value judgement, and uses that distinction to explain why honest assessors disagree. It applies the stages to the actual product rather than in the abstract, calculates a break-even number of uses when figures are supplied, resists the assumption that renewable means better, and identifies which stages a selective LCA has quietly dropped — and who benefits.
